But two pairs pull in different directions, and one is worth an explicit reconciliation.

Tensions worth reconciling

- Default tracking vs. a privacy toggle (notes 2 and 13). Note 2 says the system will track "all kinds of data of the user by default" and use that context to organize info. Note 13 says the tracking-by-default idea "needs a privacy toggle." These are not logically incompatible (default-on with an opt-out satisfies both), but the design stance shifts from "capture everything by default" to "capture, but give the user a control." Treat this as a revised decision unless you actually meant default-on plus a toggle.

- Semantic retrieval vs. embeddings deferred (notes 18 and 24). Note 18 records the project goal as a DBMS for personal notes that supports semantic retrieval, not just keyword search. Note 24 records the meeting decision with Arjun that retrieval will be lexical plus graph, with embeddings deferred to v2. Semantic retrieval is normally embeddings-based, so the v1 design as written cannot be fully semantic. This reads as a scope/phase difference (v1 = lexical + graph, semantic later) rather than a true contradiction — but if "semantic retrieval" was meant as the unqualified goal for the first version, then notes 18 and 24 do conflict and you should pick one.

Minor, within a single note

- Note 20: "argue with you about them" vs. "form opinions about them." That is self-revision inside one draft, not a cross-note contradiction.

Checked and consistent

- Java notes 3, 4, 23, and 17 agree with each other: ArrayList O(1) random access vs. LinkedList O(n) get(i) with O(1) end operations; type erasure behavior; HashMap allowing one null key and multiple null values while Hashtable allows neither; the @Transactional / @Cacheable self-invocation proxy trap. No conflicts there.
- Note 29 (spaced repetition over interpretations, with the "concepts too broad" risk) and note 30 (wanting to see which notes were used, not just cited ids) conflict with nothing in this set.
- Note 25 (Pune train, 5th out, 7th return) is standalone and unrelated to the rest.

One scoping note: per your own guidance, note 18 is your DeepNotes DBMS college project, not Java coursework — so the semantic-vs-embeddings tension in the second bullet belongs to the project track and should be kept out of Java study material.

That's the whole of what you saved; you also noted you wanted to re-read the LSP chapter.
- So your notes give the intuition but not the formal contract. What follows is general knowledge, not from your notes.
- Standard definition: objects of a subtype must be usable anywhere an object of the supertype is expected, without the caller needing to know the difference and without breaking previously correct behavior.
- Practical rules that follow: a subtype may not strengthen preconditions (accept less than the parent) or weaken postconditions (promise less than the parent); return types may be narrowed (covariant), parameter types widened (contravariant); it shouldn't throw new checked exceptions unless the parent declares them; supertype invariants must be preserved.
- Classic counterexample: letting Square extend Rectangle. A method written for Rectangle assumes setting width doesn't change height, which Square violates.
- Tiny Java-shaped example:
  class Rectangle { void setW(int w) {...} void setH(int h) {...} int area() {...} }
